title: Practice: tessellations
intro: Eight questions. The key idea every time: do the angles at a point make exactly $360^\circ$?

questions.prompt: Which of these regular polygons tessellate on their own?
hints: Check whether the interior angle divides exactly into 360.
questions.explanation: $60$, $90$ and $120$ divide into 360; $108$ and $135$ do not.

questions.prompt: Why is a pattern of circles not a tessellation?

options.text: It leaves gaps between the circles
Circles have no angles, so they cannot be measured

hints: A tessellation has no gaps and no overlaps.
questions.explanation: However you arrange circles, curved gaps are left between them.

steps.prompt: What do three of these angles add up to?

options.text: No — three leave a gap and four would overlap

questions.explanation: $3 \times 108 = 324 < 360$ and $4 \times 108 = 432 > 360$, so no whole number of pentagons fills the space.

questions.prompt: Six equal angles of equilateral triangles meet at a point in a tessellation. What is each angle?
hints: Angles at a point add to $360^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Every triangle, of any shape, will tessellate.
hints: Rotate a copy $180^\circ$ about the midpoint of a side — what shape do the two make?
questions.explanation: True. Two copies make a parallelogram, and parallelograms tessellate. At each point six angles meet — each of the triangle's three angles twice — making $2 \times 180 = 360^\circ$.

questions.prompt: Four copies of a quadrilateral with angles $132^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $71^\circ$ and $x$ meet at a point in a tessellation, one of each angle. Find $x$.
hints: The four angles of a quadrilateral add to $360^\circ$ — and so do angles at a point.

questions.prompt: Which combinations of regular polygons fit exactly round a point?

options.text: A hexagon, two squares and a triangle

questions.text: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that fit together with no [[a]] and no [[b]].
hints: Think of tiles on a floor.
